questions.question: What is EBS and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: EBS (Elastic Block Store) is AWS's persistent block storage service for EC2 instances. It solves the problem of ephemeral storage — EC2 instance store volumes are lost when an instance stops or terminates. EBS volumes are network-attached, persist independently of the EC2 lifecycle, and can be detached and reattached to different instances.

questions.question: What is the difference between Scale Up and Scale Out for EBS storage?
questions.answer: Scale Up means increasing the size or performance of an existing EBS volume (e.g., resizing from 8GB to 20GB in-place). Scale Out means adding a new, separate EBS volume alongside the existing one (e.g., attaching a fresh 12GB volume to the same EC2). Scale Up changes the existing resource; Scale Out adds new resources alongside it.

questions.question: What are the steps to attach and use a new EBS volume on a Linux EC2 instance?
questions.answer: 1. Create EBS volume in the same AZ as the EC2 instance. 2. Attach the volume to the EC2 via console (Actions → Attach Volume). 3. SSH into EC2 and verify with lsblk. 4. Format the disk with mkfs (e.g., sudo mkfs -t xfs /dev/nvme1n1). 5. Create a mount point directory (sudo mkdir /data). 6. Mount the disk (sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /data). 7. Verify with df -h. For permanent mounting, add to /etc/fstab.

questions.question: What is /etc/fstab and why is it important for EBS volumes?
questions.answer: fstab (file system table) is a Linux configuration file at /etc/fstab that defines which disks should be automatically mounted when the system boots. Without an entry in fstab, an EBS mount is temporary — it disappears after reboot. Adding the volume's UUID, mount point, file system type, and options (like nofail) to fstab makes the mount permanent and automatic.

questions.question: What is an EBS Snapshot and what makes it incremental?
questions.answer: An EBS Snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS volume stored in AWS-managed Amazon S3. It's incremental because the first snapshot captures all used data on the volume, but subsequent snapshots only store the data blocks that have changed since the previous snapshot. This makes snapshots space-efficient and cost-effective — you don't pay to store unchanged data multiple times.

questions.question: Why should you use UUID instead of device names in /etc/fstab?
questions.answer: Device names like /dev/nvme1n1 can change after a reboot or when volumes are reattached in a different order. UUIDs (Universally Unique Identifiers) are permanently assigned to each formatted file system and never change. Using UUIDs in fstab ensures the correct disk is always mounted regardless of what device name the OS assigns to it.

questions.question: What is the nofail option in fstab and why is it critical for EC2?
questions.answer: nofail is an fstab mount option that tells Linux to continue booting even if the specified disk is unavailable or fails to mount. Without nofail, if an EBS volume is detached while its fstab entry remains, the EC2 instance can get stuck in a boot loop and become inaccessible. Always use nofail for non-root EBS volumes in fstab.

questions.question: What are the EBS SSD volume types and their key differences?
questions.answer: GP2 (General Purpose v2): IOPS auto-scale with size at 3 IOPS/GB, max 16,000 IOPS. GP3 (General Purpose v3): Baseline 3,000 IOPS regardless of size, independently configurable up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s throughput. io1/io2 (Provisioned IOPS): Highest IOPS up to 64,000-256,000 for I/O-intensive databases. io2 offers 99.999% durability. GP3 is the recommended default for most workloads.

questions.question: Can an EBS volume be attached to multiple EC2 instances simultaneously?
questions.answer: Standard EBS volumes can only be attached to one EC2 instance at a time. However, EBS Multi-Attach is available for io1 and io2 volume types, allowing a single volume to be attached to up to 16 EC2 instances within the same AZ simultaneously. Multi-Attach is used for clustered databases and high-availability applications that require shared storage.

questions.question: Where are EBS Snapshots stored and who manages that storage?
questions.answer: EBS Snapshots are stored in Amazon S3, but in an AWS-managed bucket that you cannot directly access or see in your S3 console. AWS completely manages the S3 storage, replication, and durability for snapshots. You interact with snapshots only through the EC2 console, CLI, or API — not through S3 directly.

questions.question: Walk me through troubleshooting a scenario: after rebooting an EC2, a mounted EBS volume is no longer accessible at /data.
questions.answer: (Situation) After EC2 reboot, the /data mount point is empty — the 12GB EBS volume is no longer mounted. (Task) Restore access to the volume without losing any data and make the mount permanent. (Action) First ran lsblk to confirm the volume was still attached. Ran df -h to confirm /data wasn't mounted. Got the volume UUID with sudo blkid /dev/nvme1n1. Opened /etc/fstab with sudo nano and added: UUID=... /data xfs defaults,nofail 0 0. Ran sudo mount -a to test, verified with df -h. (Result) Volume mounted successfully. Tested with sudo reboot — mount persisted after reboot.

questions.question: A developer accidentally deleted all files in /data on your EC2 instance. How do you recover using EBS Snapshots?
questions.answer: (Situation) Critical data deleted from /data partition (12GB EBS volume) on a production EC2 instance. (Task) Recover all deleted files within the maintenance window. (Action) Located the most recent snapshot in EC2 → Snapshots console taken before the deletion. Created a new EBS volume from that snapshot in the same AZ as the production EC2. Attached the new volume to the EC2. Created a temporary mount point: sudo mkdir /recovery. Mounted the volume: sudo mount /dev/nvme1n2 /recovery (or with -o nouuid for XFS). Copied the needed files back: cp -r /recovery/files /data/. Detached and deleted the temporary volume after recovery. (Result) All deleted files recovered within 20 minutes from the pre-deletion snapshot.

questions.question: You need to replicate a production server to a different AWS region for disaster recovery. How would you use EBS Snapshots for this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Production EC2 in ap-south-1 (Mumbai) needs a DR copy in ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). (Task) Implement a disaster recovery strategy using snapshots. (Action) Created a snapshot of the production EC2's root EBS volume (EC2 → Volumes → Create Snapshot). Copied the snapshot to ap-southeast-1 (Actions → Copy Snapshot → select Singapore region). In Singapore, created a new EBS volume from the copied snapshot. Launched a new EC2 in Singapore using the same AMI configuration and attached the volume, or created an AMI from the snapshot directly. Configured Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to automate daily snapshot copies to Singapore. (Result) DR environment established. RTO reduced to under 30 minutes with automated daily replication.

questions.question: After attaching a fresh EBS volume to EC2, a junior engineer runs 'sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /data' and gets an error: 'wrong filesystem type, missing code page'. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Junior engineer can't mount a newly attached EBS volume. (Task) Diagnose and resolve the mount failure without losing data. (Action) Explained that a fresh EBS volume has no file system — it's a raw, unformatted disk. The OS can't mount it because it doesn't know how to read it. The fix is to format it first: sudo mkfs -t xfs /dev/nvme1n1 (warning: this erases any data, which is fine for a new empty disk). Then mount: sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /data. Explained the difference between XFS and EXT4 and helped them add a permanent fstab entry. (Result) Volume mounted successfully. Used the opportunity to teach about disk formatting and file system types.

questions.question: You restore an XFS snapshot to a new EC2 instance and get a UUID conflict error when mounting. What is causing this and how do you resolve it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Restored EBS snapshot (XFS formatted) cannot be mounted on a new EC2 — UUID conflict error. (Task) Mount the volume and access the data. (Action) Explained the root cause: when you create a volume from an XFS snapshot, the new volume inherits the original volume's XFS UUID. When the new EC2 sees a volume with the same UUID as another mounted volume (or sees it as a duplicate from the same system), XFS blocks the mount to prevent corruption. Solution: mount with the -o nouuid option to bypass UUID checking: sudo mount -o nouuid /dev/nvme1n1 /data. Alternatively, generate a new UUID with xfs_admin -U generate /dev/nvme1n1 before mounting. (Result) Volume mounted successfully and data accessible. Documented both solutions in the runbook.

questions.question: A product manager asks: 'We're spending too much on EBS snapshot storage. How can we reduce costs?' What do you recommend?
questions.answer: (Situation) EBS snapshot storage costs are high due to unmanaged accumulation of old snapshots. (Task) Reduce snapshot storage costs while maintaining adequate backup coverage. (Action) Analyzed existing snapshots — found many volumes had daily snapshots going back 18 months with no retention policy. Implemented Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) with policies: daily snapshots retained for 7 days, weekly snapshots retained for 4 weeks, monthly snapshots retained for 3 months. Deleted all snapshots outside the new retention window. Enabled incremental snapshots (already default). Moved older snapshots to EBS Snapshot Archive for 75% cost reduction on rarely-accessed snapshots. (Result) Storage costs reduced by 60% within the first month while maintaining 3-month recovery capability.

questions.question: What is the difference between taking a snapshot of a specific EBS volume versus creating an image (AMI) from an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: (Situation) Developer unsure whether to use snapshot or AMI for a backup strategy. (Task) Explain the difference and recommend the right approach. (Action) Explained: A volume snapshot backs up just the data on that disk — it's a data backup. You can restore a volume from it but cannot directly launch a new EC2 from a single volume snapshot. An AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is a complete server template — it includes one or more EBS snapshots PLUS boot configuration (kernel, block device mappings, architecture). From an AMI, you can launch identical EC2 instances. (Result) Recommended: use volume snapshots for routine data backup and disaster recovery of data. Use AMIs when you need to clone a full server configuration or enable auto-scaling with pre-configured instances.

questions.question: How would you verify that an /etc/fstab entry is correct before rebooting an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: (Situation) New fstab entry added for a 12GB EBS volume — need to verify before rebooting. (Task) Test the fstab entry without risking a failed reboot. (Action) First unmount the disk: sudo umount /data. Then run sudo mount -a — this reads /etc/fstab and mounts everything listed that isn't already mounted. If there's a typo or error, it shows immediately without rebooting. Verified with df -h that /data appeared with 12GB available. This approach catches fstab errors before they can cause a boot failure. (Result) Fstab entry confirmed correct. Proceeded with the reboot confidently.

questions.question: Explain EBS volume encryption and when you would enable it. Can you encrypt an existing unencrypted volume?
questions.answer: EBS volumes can be encrypted at rest using AWS KMS (Key Management Service). Encryption covers data stored on the volume, data moving between the volume and EC2, and all snapshots. You should enable encryption for any volume storing sensitive data (PII, financial records, HIPAA data) and in regulated environments. To encrypt an existing unencrypted volume: take a snapshot of the unencrypted volume → copy the snapshot with encryption enabled → create a new volume from the encrypted copy → swap out the old volume. You cannot encrypt a volume in-place.

questions.question: What happens to EBS data when you stop, terminate, or reboot an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: Stop: EBS root and data volumes persist — data is safe. Instance store volumes are wiped. EC2 can be restarted and data is available. Reboot: All EBS volumes remain attached and mounted — data persists as if the OS was just restarted. Terminate: By default, the root EBS volume is deleted (DeleteOnTermination=true). Additional EBS volumes that were manually attached typically persist (DeleteOnTermination=false by default). You can change DeleteOnTermination settings before termination to preserve or delete volumes as needed.

questions.question: Design a cost-optimized backup strategy for a company with 50 EC2 instances in production. Requirements: 7-day point-in-time recovery, 1-year retention for compliance, and minimal cost.
questions.answer: For 7-day point-in-time recovery with 1-year compliance retention, I would design a tiered strategy: Layer 1 — Daily snapshots with Amazon DLM: take automated daily snapshots of all 50 instances, retain the last 7 snapshots per volume for point-in-time recovery. Cost: pay for 7x used-data per volume. Layer 2 — Weekly archival: use EBS Snapshot Archive for snapshots older than 7 days. Archive pricing is ~75% cheaper than standard snapshot storage. Keep weekly snapshots for the remaining 51 weeks to meet the 1-year requirement. Layer 3 — Cross-region copy for DR: copy monthly snapshots to a secondary region for disaster resilience. Tag all snapshots with retention metadata. Total cost estimate: significantly lower than keeping all daily snapshots at full price for 1 year. DLM handles creation, retention, and deletion automatically — no manual management required.

questions.question: An application writes data to multiple EBS volumes simultaneously. How do you ensure snapshot consistency across all volumes?
questions.answer: For multi-volume application consistency, the challenge is that snapshots taken at different times capture volumes at different states — if your database has data volume and transaction log volume, an inconsistent snapshot could lead to corruption on restore. Solutions: Option 1 — EC2-level multi-volume snapshot: use 'Create Snapshot' on the EC2 Instance (not individual volumes) — AWS creates coordinated snapshots of all attached volumes at the same instant. Option 2 — Quiesce the application: pause writes (using application-level commands, fsfreeze on Linux, or VSS on Windows) before taking snapshots, then resume. Option 3 — AWS Backup: provides application-consistent snapshots for databases and complex workloads. For production databases, always quiesce or use application-aware backup tools.

questions.question: Compare and contrast GP3 and io2 Block Express — when would you choose each for a high-traffic database workload?
questions.answer: GP3: Max 16,000 IOPS, max 1,000 MiB/s throughput, up to 16TB, 99.8-99.9% durability. Cost: ~$0.08/GB/month + $0.005/IOPS above 3,000. Best for: most web applications, development databases, medium-traffic production databases, any workload needing up to 16,000 IOPS. io2 Block Express: Max 256,000 IOPS, max 4,000 MiB/s throughput, up to 64TB, 99.999% durability. Supports Multi-Attach. Cost: ~$0.125/GB/month + $0.065/IOPS. Best for: mission-critical databases (Oracle, SAP HANA, SQL Server), sub-millisecond latency requirements, workloads exceeding 16,000 IOPS, applications requiring five-nines durability. Decision: use GP3 as the default and only upgrade to io2 Block Express when IOPS requirements exceed 16,000 or when sub-millisecond consistent latency is required.

questions.question: Explain how EBS Multi-Attach works and what architectural patterns it enables.
questions.answer: EBS Multi-Attach allows a single io1 or io2 EBS volume to be attached to up to 16 EC2 instances simultaneously within the same Availability Zone. All instances have full read/write access to the same volume. Use cases: clustered databases (like Oracle RAC) that require shared storage, high-availability application clusters where multiple nodes need access to the same data, fault-tolerant architectures where a standby instance can immediately access the primary's data if the primary fails. Limitations: only within the same AZ (not cross-AZ), only with io1/io2 volumes, applications must manage concurrent write coordination to avoid corruption (the OS/app must be cluster-aware). Not a replacement for distributed file systems like Amazon EFS for general shared storage.

questions.question: Walk through the complete architecture for a disaster recovery solution using EBS Snapshots with an RTO of under 1 hour and RPO of under 4 hours.
questions.answer: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) of 4 hours means we take snapshots every 4 hours — data loss limited to at most 4 hours. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) of 1 hour means we must be fully operational within 1 hour of a disaster. Architecture: Step 1 — Automated snapshots with DLM: configure DLM policies to snapshot all production EBS volumes every 4 hours. Tag snapshots with application name and timestamp. Step 2 — Cross-region replication: configure DLM to automatically copy each snapshot to the DR region (e.g., Mumbai primary → Singapore DR) within 30 minutes. Step 3 — Pre-warm EC2 in DR region: maintain stopped EC2 instances in the DR region pre-configured with the right instance types, security groups, and VPC — stopping them when not in a DR event. Step 4 — Runbooks: document exact steps for DR activation — volume creation from snapshot, EC2 start, DNS failover (Route 53). Target: snapshot creation (15 min) + cross-region copy (20 min) + DR activation (25 min) = well within 1 hour RTO. Step 5 — Regular DR drills: test the entire process quarterly to validate actual RTO/RPO under real conditions.
